title: Procedural Terrain Generation in Unity (Rivers, Roads, and A*)
description: A look at a group project where we built a procedural terrain generator using Perlin noise, greedy search, and A* pathfinding.

content.text: This was a group project I worked on, and it was honestly one of my favorite projects I’ve done. It was very open-ended — we were basically allowed to build whatever we wanted — and I think that freedom is what made it turn into something I’m actually proud of.

The idea was to create a terrain generator for Dungeons & Dragons campaigns. I’m not really a huge D&D person, but I do really like procedural terrain generation, so that was the part that hooked me immediately.
Tech Stack (Why Unity?)
We built the project in Unity. It made a lot of sense for this kind of problem because we could quickly visualize terrain, iterate on ideas, and actually see how the generation changed in real time.
Being able to tweak parameters and instantly see the results is huge when working on procedural systems. Without that, you’re basically guessing.
Breaking the Problem Down
We ended up splitting the project into three main parts:

1. Base terrain generation
2. Water features (rivers and lakes)
3. Roads connecting important locations
Base Terrain (Perlin Noise)
For the terrain itself, we didn’t do anything too crazy. We used Perlin noise to generate a heightmap.

Perlin noise is nice because it gives you smooth, natural-looking variation instead of completely random values. So instead of jagged chaos, you get rolling hills, valleys, and more realistic terrain.
At a high level, you sample a noise function at each (x, y) coordinate and treat the result as elevation. That’s basically your world.
Water Generation (Greedy Search)
Water was a bit more interesting. We wanted rivers to feel somewhat natural, not just random lines.
We used a greedy approach because it actually maps pretty well to how water behaves. At each step, the algorithm just picks the lowest neighboring point — basically “go downhill as much as possible.”
So the idea looks like this:

• Start from a high elevation point
• Look at neighboring tiles
• Move to the one with the lowest height
• Repeat until you hit an ocean or a basin
This creates paths that naturally flow downhill, which ends up looking pretty convincing.
We also handled things like local minimums by letting water pool and then branch out into new paths. That helped avoid rivers just getting stuck awkwardly.
What Is a Greedy Algorithm?
A greedy algorithm is one that makes the best local decision at each step, without worrying about the bigger picture.
In our case, the "best" choice was simply "go to the lowest adjacent tile." It doesn’t plan ahead — it just reacts to what’s immediately available.
This doesn’t always give a globally optimal result, but for something like water flow, it actually works really well.
Road Generation (A*)
Roads were the part I worked on. The goal was to connect important locations (like cities) in a way that felt realistic.
My thinking was: people build roads to connect points efficiently. They might avoid mountains or water, but they’re still trying to minimize cost overall.
That’s basically what A* is designed for.
What Is A*?
A* is a pathfinding algorithm that finds the lowest-cost path between two points. It’s like a smarter version of Dijkstra’s algorithm.
It works by combining two values:

g(n): the cost to reach the current node
h(n): a heuristic estimate of the cost to reach the goal
Then it evaluates nodes using:
f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
This lets it prioritize paths that are both cheap so far and likely to stay cheap.
Our Heuristics
We used a few different factors to influence road generation:

• Distance heuristic: encourages shorter paths
• Elevation heuristic: avoids steep terrain
• Water heuristic: discourages crossing rivers or lakes
For distance, we used a grid-based approximation like:
(Δx + Δy) - min(Δx, Δy)
This works well for grid movement and keeps the path fairly direct.
All of these combined gave us roads that felt pretty natural — not perfectly realistic, but definitely believable.
Putting It All Together
So the full pipeline looked something like:

1. Generate terrain with Perlin noise
2. Add oceans and base elevation
3. Generate rivers using greedy descent
4. Connect locations with A* roads
Each step builds on the previous one, which made the whole system feel pretty cohesive.

Conclusion
This project was fun because it didn’t feel like a strict assignment. It felt like building something I actually cared about.
It also helped me understand how different algorithms can map to real-world behavior — like greedy search for water and A* for human-made paths.
And honestly, just seeing everything come together visually in Unity made it way more satisfying than just writing algorithms on paper.
